page: Amazon Web Services c6gd.xlarge is a compute-optimized instance powered by a custom 64-bit ARM architecture. It features an AWS Graviton processor utilizing the Neoverse-N1 microarchitecture, operating at a dedicated frequency of 2.5 GHz. The instance provides 4 physical cores and 4 vCPUs with a single thread per core, meaning hyperthreading is disabled. It is equipped with 8.0 GB of system memory, yielding a 2.0 GB per core ratio, and includes a 237 GB local NVMe SSD instance store volume.

Benchmark data indicates average performance for compute-heavy workloads, with stress-ng single-core and multi-core CPU tests scoring 1519.58 and 6061.97 respectively. Large-block memory bandwidth is moderate, reaching 72.54 GB/sec for read operations and 33.66 GB/sec for write operations. However, the instance exhibits weaker performance in memory-bound or complex instruction tasks, as shown by a Geekbench single-core score of 932.0 and a Passmark CPU score of 2694.32. Cryptographic acceleration is supported via hardware AES, though advanced vector extensions are absent.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the c6gd.xlarge offers a balanced profile for ARM-native workloads requiring dedicated compute resources and fast local scratch space without the overhead of network-attached storage. The 1 Gbps baseline network bandwidth limits high-throughput network applications. This instance is suited for distributed compute tasks, application servers, local database operations, and lightweight containerized microservices that benefit from local NVMe storage and dedicated ARM cores.
description: The Amazon Web Services c6gd.xlarge is a compute-optimized instance featuring 4 dedicated physical cores on a 2.5 GHz ARM64 AWS Graviton Neoverse-N1 processor. It is configured with 8.0 GB of system memory and a 237 GB local NVMe SSD instance store volume, running on the Nitro hypervisor. Performance benchmarks show average results for standard compute tasks, with stress-ng single-core and multi-core scores of 1519.58 and 6061.97, alongside moderate large-block memory write speeds of 33.66 GB/sec. However, it exhibits lower performance in complex instruction sets and text processing due to the lack of AVX extensions. With a 1 Gbps baseline network bandwidth, this instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for ARM-native workloads, local database operations, and lightweight web serving that require dedicated CPU resources and fast local scratch storage.
